title: Dermatitis herpetiformis & coeliac disease
summary: An intensely itchy, symmetrical eruption of tiny blisters on the elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp that is the skin form of coeliac disease. Test for coeliac disease while still eating gluten; a strict gluten-free diet is the long-term treatment.

glance.think: Intense itch with grouped tiny vesicles or just excoriations on the elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp, not responding to steroids.
glance.engine: Gluten sensitivity: IgA against epidermal transglutaminase deposits in the dermal papillae (granular IgA on DIF).
glance.backbone: Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) before any gluten-free trial; refer for biopsy with DIF; lifelong gluten-free diet; specialist dapsone for itch control.
glance.never_miss: Anaemia, osteoporosis and small-bowel lymphoma risk; G6PD check and haemolysis/methaemoglobinaemia on dapsone.

what: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the **skin form of coeliac disease**. It is an intensely itchy, chronic, grouped papulovesicular eruption on the extensor surfaces, caused by gluten sensitivity. Almost all patients have gluten-sensitive enteropathy on biopsy, even though **most have few or no gut symptoms** (or symptoms labelled "IBS", as in Cases 2 and 4). It mostly affects people of Northern European descent aged 30–40 and is slightly commoner in men. It is rare in children, and in Japanese and African-heritage populations.
The **skin manifestation of coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy)**: an intensely itchy, symmetrical papulovesicular eruption on the extensor surfaces.

list: It affects ~10–20% of coeliac patients; adults aged 30–40 are typical; M ≥ F (unlike coeliac overall).
**Most have coeliac enteropathy on biopsy**, though GI symptoms are often absent or mild. **This case has bloating, malaise and weight loss.**

cause: Genetic background is **HLA-DQ2/DQ8**. Gliadin is deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (TG2), which drives mucosal IgA anti-TG2 and then, by epitope spreading, IgA against **epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)**. IgA–TG3 complexes deposit in the **dermal papillae**, neutrophils gather into papillary microabscesses, and a subepidermal vesicle forms. Iodide (e.g. iodinated contrast or seaweed) and NSAIDs can make it flare.

list: In genetically predisposed people (**HLA-DQ2/DQ8**), gluten triggers IgA autoantibodies to tissue transglutaminase (**TG2**, gut) and **epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)**.
**IgA–TG3 complexes deposit in the dermal papillae** → neutrophil recruitment → subepidermal vesicles.
Iodine and NSAIDs can flare it.

Associations: autoimmune thyroid disease, T1DM, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, alopecia areata, Sjögren's; **small-bowel (enteropathy-associated T-cell) lymphoma** (risk reduced by a gluten-free diet).
**Symmetrical extensor distribution:** **elbows, forearms, knees, buttocks/sacrum, shoulders, scalp**.

**Intense itch or burning**, often before lesions appear. Tiny vesicles are scratched off quickly, so patients usually present with **excoriations, crusted erosions and post-inflammatory change only** (Case 4: "excoriations without blisters"; photo C04).

Associated features: **gut:** bloating, loose stool, "IBS" (Cases 2 and 4); **iron-deficiency anaemia or pallor** (Case 2); aphthae, dental enamel defects, fatigue; personal or family history of autoimmunity (thyroid disease, T1DM, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo)
Case 2's atopic history is a **red herring** that steers people toward "eczema". Case 4's **failure of Betnovate** (TCS barely touches DH) and the **normal routine bloods** are also typical.

Grouped ("herpetiform") **small vesicles and papules**, usually seen as **excoriations, erosions and crusts** because the itch is intense — patients scratch the vesicles off. Post-inflammatory pigment change.
Symmetrical on the **elbows/extensor forearms, knees, buttocks/sacrum**, shoulders, and **scalp/posterior hairline**; facial and palmar purpura (rare).
Mucosa is usually spared.
**Systemic/GI:** bloating, diarrhoea, weight loss, malaise; iron/folate deficiency; dental enamel defects; osteoporosis.

ol: **Coeliac serology while the patient is eating gluten** (NICE NG20): **IgA tissue transglutaminase (tTG-IgA) + total IgA** first line. Use IgA **EMA** if tTG is weakly positive, and IgG-based tests (IgG tTG/DGP/EMA) if IgA-deficient. Advise eating gluten in **more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks** before testing. In DH, serology is positive in ~75–90%, so a negative result doesn't exclude it.

**Skin biopsy for DIF from perilesional, uninvolved skin** (about 1 cm from a lesion, ideally on the buttock or forearm; *not* lesional skin, where inflammation destroys the IgA). It shows **granular IgA in the dermal papillae**, which is the **diagnostic gold standard**. Lesional H&E (if an intact vesicle exists) shows a subepidermal blister with papillary neutrophil microabscesses.

**Gastroenterology:** NICE NG20 says to refer anyone with DH for specialist assessment. Whether a duodenal biopsy is needed in proven DH is decided by gastroenterology and dermatology together (many UK centres skip it when skin DIF is positive).
**Baseline bloods:** FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, calcium/vitamin D/ALP, LFT, TFT, glucose; **G6PD before dapsone**. Consider a DXA scan (NG20 criteria).

list: **Skin biopsy is the gold standard**: **perilesional, normal-looking skin** (~1 cm from a lesion) for **DIF** — **granular IgA in the dermal papillae**. Send it in **Michel's transport medium or saline, not formalin**; ± **lesional biopsy in formalin** for H&E: subepidermal blister with **neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae**; Usually done by dermatology

**Coeliac serology** (NICE NG20): **tTG-IgA + total IgA**. If IgA-deficient, use IgG-based tests (tTG-IgG, DGP-IgG or EMA-IgG); EMA-IgA if tTG is equivocal; epidermal TG3 antibodies (specialist); **The patient must be eating gluten** — **in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks** before testing. Ask before any gluten-free trial (course teaching: "prep to the test")
**Other investigations:** FBC, **ferritin, folate, B12**, LFT, U&E, calcium, **vitamin D**, TFT (autoimmune thyroid), HbA1c; **DEXA** if risk factors or at diagnosis per BSG; **G6PD** before dapsone
A **duodenal biopsy is usually not required** when DH is confirmed on skin biopsy (BSG 2014), though GI referral may still be needed for significant GI symptoms, red flags or uncertainty.
**Scabies** (burrows, web spaces, genitals, contacts; Case 4 specifically had **no burrows**)
**atopic or nummular eczema** (Case 2's atopic history)
**neurotic excoriations or prurigo**
**papular urticaria / insect bites**
**linear IgA disease** (linear IgA on DIF, no coeliac link, often drug-induced)
**BP** (older patient, tense bullae)
**folliculitis**
**Grover's** (trunk, older men)
**scabies + DH both possible**

differentials: **Scabies** (burrows, finger webs, genitals, contacts itchy), **atopic/nummular eczema**, **papular urticaria/insect bites**, **linear IgA disease** (linear IgA on DIF; drug-induced — vancomycin), **bullous pemphigoid** (older, tense bullae, linear IgG/C3), neurotic excoriations/prurigo, folliculitis, **eruptive xanthoma** (see *Eruptive xanthomas — new diabetes* — same sites, the course DDx), psoriasis (elbows/knees), herpes zoster/simplex (unilateral, grouped).

list: **Immediate management:** **do not start a gluten-free diet yet**; keep eating gluten until serology and biopsy are done. **Refer to dermatology** for biopsy with DIF, and to **gastroenterology** (NICE NG20). Meanwhile, symptomatic relief with emollients, a sedating antihistamine at night (limited benefit), and a potent TCS for short-term itch relief only (expect little response).

**Best skin drug: dapsone** (specialist-initiated, then shared care): Typical start is 25–50 mg daily, titrated to the lowest dose that controls itch (often 50–100 mg). Itch responds within **48–72 h**, which also supports the diagnosis; **Pre-checks:** G6PD (risk of severe haemolysis if deficient), FBC, LFT, U&E; **Monitoring:** FBC **weekly for 4 weeks, then every 2 weeks to 12 weeks, then 3-monthly**, plus LFT and reticulocytes per the local shared-care protocol. Every patient has **dose-related haemolysis** and **methaemoglobinaemia** (blue-grey lips, breathlessness, headache). Rarer but serious: **agranulocytosis** (usually weeks 3–12, so counsel about sore throat, fever and mouth ulcers → urgent FBC), **dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome / DRESS** (weeks 2–6; HLA-B*13:01), hepatitis, and peripheral motor neuropathy; Interactions: trimethoprim raises levels, rifampicin lowers them, and other oxidant drugs add to haemolysis; **Alternatives:** **sulfapyridine** (unlicensed, import or specials) or **sulfamethoxypyridazine**; **sulfasalazine** is sometimes used. Superpotent TCS as an adjunct for lesions

**Lifestyle:** **lifelong strict gluten-free diet (GFD)**, which is the definitive treatment. It lets dapsone be reduced or stopped, usually after **1–2 years** (the skin lags behind the gut), and lowers the risk of lymphoma. Wheat, barley, rye and cross-contaminated oats are excluded; uncontaminated oats are allowed for most. Refer to a **dietitian**, and offer **Coeliac UK** membership. Gluten-free food prescribing varies across the UK (e.g. England restricted it to bread and mixes in 2018, and ICBs vary).

**Complications to screen for or counsel about:** **enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma and other NHL** (risk falls with strict GFD); small-bowel adenocarcinoma (rare); **osteoporosis/osteopenia** (calcium, vitamin D, DXA per NICE); **iron, folate and B12 deficiency**; **autoimmune thyroid disease, T1DM**, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, alopecia areata; **hyposplenism** (NG20: consider pneumococcal and other vaccines); reduced fertility and adverse pregnancy outcomes if untreated; **dapsone toxicity**; psychosocial burden of the diet; first-degree relatives have ~10% risk (offer serology if symptomatic; NG20)

ol: **Lifelong strict gluten-free diet (GFD)** — first-line and essential. It treats the enteropathy, eventually controls the rash (**itch improves over months; full skin remission can take 6 months–2 years**), lets dapsone be withdrawn, and **lowers lymphoma risk**. Refer to a **dietitian**; Coeliac UK membership. Gluten-free food prescriptions vary by ICB in England (many have withdrawn them) and are free in Wales/Scotland.

**Dapsone** for rapid symptom control (itch settles within 48–72 h), specialist-initiated: **Check G6PD first.** Start 25–50 mg daily and titrate (usually ≤100–200 mg); **Haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia** (dose-related, near universal) — breathlessness, cyanosis, fatigue; **Agranulocytosis** (mainly in the first 3 months — sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers → urgent FBC); **Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome** (DRESS-like, weeks 3–6; HLA-B*13:01 in Asian patients), hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy; **Monitoring (BNF/local shared care):** FBC (incl. reticulocytes/methaemoglobin as indicated) and LFT, e.g. weekly for the first month, then monthly for 6 months, then 6-monthly; Alternatives if intolerant: sulfapyridine/sulfamethoxypyridazine (limited availability), potent topical steroids, antihistamines (minor benefit)

**Coeliac follow-up (NICE NG20/BSG):** annual review (weight, symptoms, diet adherence, **tTG** to monitor adherence, FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, LFT, TFT, bone health); **pneumococcal vaccination** (hyposplenism — BSG); calcium/vitamin D; **offer serological testing to first-degree relatives**.
**Avoid** iodine-containing preparations, ideally, NSAIDs if they trigger flares.

management: Suspected DH (dermatology for biopsy with DIF); weight loss, anaemia, dysphagia or persistent GI symptoms despite GFD (gastroenterology — exclude refractory coeliac disease/lymphoma); symptoms of dapsone toxicity (urgent bloods); new lymphadenopathy, night sweats or abdominal pain (lymphoma).

Coeliac serology (while the patient is still eating gluten), baseline bloods, dietary counselling and referral, symptomatic topical steroid/antihistamine, shared-care dapsone monitoring (where locally agreed), and family testing.
red_flags: Do not start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy: it gives false-negative results.
On dapsone: check G6PD first; watch for haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia (blue lips, breathlessness), agranulocytosis and DRESS.
Weight loss, anaemia or diarrhoea: gastroenterology (NICE NG20).
pearls: **"Itchy elbows and buttocks plus 'IBS' or anaemia" means DH.** Test before the patient tries a gluten-free diet on their own (Case 4's dietitian referral could start this by accident; tell the dietitian).
Check excipients: wheat starch in tablet excipients is usually at negligible gluten levels (per BNF/Coeliac UK), but counsel patients who ask.
Dapsone: **record the G6PD result before the first dose**, give written agranulocytosis and methaemoglobinaemia warnings, and do not issue repeats without up-to-date bloods.
An annual coeliac review covers weight, symptoms, diet adherence, dietitian referral if needed, and bloods.
"**Itchy elbows, knees and buttocks with excoriations and no intact blisters = think DH — and don't let them go gluten-free before testing.**"
Dapsone brings quick relief, but **the diet is the treatment**.
Total IgA, always — IgA deficiency (~2–3% of coeliac patients) gives false-negative tTG-IgA.
